definition.text: The close link between climate change and poverty, since climate change hits poor people and developing countries hardest.

facts.text: Poor people face more exposure and vulnerability, meaning they are less able to cope with climate extremes.
The UN Development Programme says developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change.
A 2020 World Bank paper estimated climate change will push 32 million to 132 million more people into extreme poverty by 2030.
For poor households, a disaster, a bad harvest or an illness can be a crippling economic shock.
Climate-driven extremes could raise food prices by 3–84% by 2050.
Pro-poor adaptation links adaptation to poverty reduction; adaptation that ignores how poverty differs between people will be ineffective and unfair.
Poorer countries are hit harder yet have fewer assets and capacities to adapt.

definition.text: The idea that rich Global North countries have taken over most of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb greenhouse gases, leaving the Global South to bear the consequences.

facts.text: Global North countries, with 19% of world population, account for 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions; the Global South accounts for 8%.
Countries such as Ecuador emit relatively little carbon dioxide but have far fewer resources to cope with local climate impacts.

title: Climate apartheid
article: Climate change and poverty#Human rights and democracy

definition.text: A situation in which only the rich can escape the consequences of climate change.

facts.text: UN Special Rapporteur Philip Alston warned of it in June 2019, saying it could undermine human rights, democracy and the rule of law.
He cited Superstorm Sandy in 2012, when most of New York lost power while Goldman Sachs's headquarters had its own generator and sandbags.

definition.text: A conservation movement from the 1980s that involves local communities in protecting nature, in reaction to top-down conservation that ignored them.

facts.text: It grew out of opposition to fortress conservation, under which more than 20 million people are estimated to have been displaced.
In 1975 the IUCN first accepted that traditional ways of life could support biodiversity conservation.
The 2003 World Parks Congress and a 2004 CBD meeting recognised Indigenous peoples and local communities as governors of protected areas.
Co-management shares responsibility for protected areas between the state and local communities, blending traditional knowledge with science.
Livelihood strategies include ecotourism, rotational grazing, non-timber forest products, sustainable fisheries and carbon projects.
Community-managed lands in parts of Kenya have shown higher nutrient levels and plant productivity.
Benefits are often captured by local elites, while costs such as lost access to land fall on poorer households, as in Madagascar.
Legal recognition of communal land rights is essential for long-term success.
